pages.text:
*Rule 2 of the Library at the Bottom of the Sea: A library is only closed when its last reader stops coming.*

The Saltmarrow Library lived in an old customs house that looked exactly like a giant upturned boat. It sat on the cobblestones with its curved roof rising like a hull, and the door creaked with a long, wooden sigh every time it opened. Inside, the air smelled of old paper and dried salt, a scent Wren loved more than any chocolate biscuit.

Mrs. Pell stood by the desk, her white curls puffing like sea foam. Her tortoiseshell glasses slid down her nose on a beaded chain. She saw Wren, who was still in her yellow rubber boots, and gave a small, silent nod. She did not ask about homework. She did not ask about the stomachache. She just pointed to the reading nook, tucked safely in the curve of the hull, and went back to stamping a return with a heavy *chunk*.

Wren slipped into the nook. The wood was warm and smooth, shaped by years of small backs leaning against it. She tapped the rhythm of her heartbeat on her knee and settled in, feeling the whole world fall away.
pages.image: Interior of a library shaped like an upturned boat hull; Wren, a ten-year-old girl with short black curls in a coral-red sweater, blue overalls, and yellow boots, sits in a cozy curved reading nook while Mrs. Pell, an elderly woman with white curls and glasses, stands by a desk in the background.

pages.text:
Mrs. Pell did not make Wren read aloud. Not once. Not even when the words swam and wriggled like minnows in the shallow end. Instead, she would climb into the nook with a book under her arm, settle her long grey skirt, and read to her. Her voice was soft and dry, like sandpaper on a smooth stone, but it made the stories land right in the middle of Wren’s chest.

When Mrs. Pell finished, she would close the book and wait.

Then Wren would tell it back. Every word. Every pause. The way the goat blinked. The way the lighthouse keeper coughed. She could do it without looking at the page, without a single letter swimming away.

Mrs. Pell would smile, a tiny crinkle appearing by her eyes. "That is reading too, dear," she would say, tapping the cover of the book. "It is just reading by ear first." And Wren would feel her shoulders drop, the knot in her stomach loosening just enough to let her breathe.
pages.image: Mrs. Pell, an elderly woman in a plum-purple cardigan, sits in a boat-shaped reading nook reading a book to Wren, a girl with short black curls in a coral-red sweater, who leans forward listening intently with a bright, happy expression.

pages.text:
On the door, pinned right at eye level, was a notice. It was yellow, official, and very flat. It said that the Harbor Council would vote on the last day of summer. If they voted yes, the library would close. The building would be sold.

Mr. Hollis Grubb, the chair of the Council, stopped to tie his shoelace. He was heavyset, with a big grey mustache that twitched when he was worried. He wore a brown tweed suit that looked too small for him, and a gold watch chain that clinked against his belt.

"Terrible leak in the roof," he said, not looking up. "Costs are up. It is a budget thing, really." He stood up, brushed a speck of dust from his knee, and walked away without waiting for an answer.

Mrs. Pell straightened her cardigan. She did not say anything. She just picked up a stray thread and held it between her fingers, her face as calm as the surface of the harbor at noon.
pages.image: A bright yellow notice is pinned to the wooden door of a boat-shaped building; Mr. Grubb, a heavyset man with a grey mustache in a brown tweed suit, looks down at his shoes while Wren, in a coral-red sweater, watches him with a worried look.

pages.text:
In the poetry corner, a small bucket sat on the floor, catching the steady, cold drips from the ceiling with a sound like *plip, plip, plip*. The water smelled of rain and old wood, and it had been there for weeks, growing heavier until the bucket was nearly full. Wren watched the ripples spread and settle, then spread again, while a single drop hovered on a beam of dust, waiting. She wanted to ask Mrs. Pell if they could fix it, but she knew the answer before she asked because the money was in the Council’s pockets, or the Mayor’s, or somewhere else where Wren’s yellow boots couldn’t reach.

"Books don’t close, dear," Mrs. Pell said quietly. She was shelving a book, her movements slow and sure, and she did not look at the bucket. "People just stop opening them."

Wren looked at the bucket again. It was full now. One more drop, and it would spill over the poetry, and the words would swim away for good.
pages.image: A small metal bucket catches water dripping from the ceiling in a dim corner of a library; Wren, a girl with short black curls, stands beside it looking concerned, while Mrs. Pell, in a purple cardigan, shelves a book in the background.

pages.text:
Wren walked home along the sea wall, the wind pulling at her coral-red sweater. The old white Saltmarrow Light stood on the rocks, silent and tall. Her boots squeaked on the wet stones. She was angry. She was sad. She was ten years old, and she had no idea how a girl who couldn’t read could save a library.

But she tapped the rhythm on her knee anyway. One for the leak. Two for the vote. Three for the words that swam.

She promised herself, right there on the wall, that she would fix it. She didn’t know how. She didn’t have money. She didn’t have a magic wand. But she had her ears, and she had her memory, and she had a secret she was just beginning to suspect: the sea had heard everything, and maybe, just maybe, it had something to say back.
pages.image: Wren, a girl with short black curls in a coral-red sweater and yellow boots, walks along a wet stone sea wall with a white lighthouse on the rocks behind her, her face set in a determined, slightly angry expression against the grey sky.
